cards.title: Rebirth of the individual
cards.body: The Renaissance (roughly 1400-1600) was Europe's great reboot. After centuries of flat, symbolic medieval art, painters rediscovered the human body, real space, and the individual. Art stopped being only about heaven and started being about people — their muscles, their faces, their world.

cards.title: Perspective changed everything
cards.body: The Renaissance's superpower was linear perspective: parallel lines converging at a vanishing point to create believable depth. Brunelleschi worked out the math, and painters like Masaccio turned flat walls into windows. For the first time, you could feel like you were standing inside the painting.

Look at Leonardo's Last Supper: the architecture's lines all converge behind Christ's head, pulling your eye exactly where Leonardo wants it. The vanishing point isn't just geometry — it's a spotlight. Every Renaissance master used this trick to direct your attention.

Spot a Renaissance painting fast: realistic bodies with weight and shadow, deep architectural space, and classical references (columns, togas, myths). If the figures look like they could step off the wall, you're in the right century.

cards.q: What did linear perspective give Renaissance painters?
choices: Believable depth — flat surfaces that look like real space
cards.explain: Perspective's converging lines create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface — the defining technical leap of the era.

flashcards.back: A technique where parallel lines converge at a vanishing point to create believable depth.

flashcards.front: Name the painter of the Last Supper.
How do you spot a Renaissance painting?
flashcards.back: Realistic bodies with weight and shadow, deep space, classical references — figures that feel alive.

questions.q: The Renaissance marked a shift from:
choices: Symbolic medieval art toward realistic, human-centered art
questions.explain: Medieval art was flat and symbolic, serving theology. The Renaissance revived classical realism and put humans — bodies, faces, minds — at the center.

questions.q: Who is credited with working out the mathematics of perspective?
questions.explain: Filippo Brunelleschi, an architect, demonstrated linear perspective around 1415. Painters ran with it immediately.

questions.q: In the Last Supper, the perspective lines converge:
questions.explain: Leonardo aimed every architectural line at Christ's head — geometry as a spotlight, the most famous vanishing point in art.

questions.q: Which is NOT a Renaissance hallmark?
choices: Flat gold backgrounds with no depth
questions.explain: Flat gold backgrounds are medieval. Renaissance painters replaced them with deep space, real bodies, and classical references.

questions.q: Besides painting, the Renaissance is famous for reviving:
questions.explain: 'Renaissance' means rebirth — of classical antiquity's art, science, and human-centered thinking, all feeding each other.

cards.title: Painting the light, not the thing
cards.body: Impressionism (1860s-1880s, mostly France) broke the biggest rule in art: finish your painting carefully in a studio. Instead, Monet, Renoir, and friends dragged easels outdoors and painted fast, capturing how light looked at one exact moment — a sunrise, a ripple, a shadow at 5pm.

cards.title: Broken color
cards.body: Up close, an Impressionist canvas is a mess of separate dabs — blue next to orange, purple beside yellow. Step back and your eye mixes them into shimmering light. They stopped blending paint on the palette and started blending it in the viewer's eye. The name came from a critic's insult: 'just an impression.'

Monet painted Rouen Cathedral more than 30 times — same building, different hours, different weather. Morning fog turns it blue-grey; sunset sets it ablaze in orange. The subject barely matters; the series is really 30 studies of light itself.

Spot Impressionism fast: visible brushstrokes, unblended dabs of pure color, everyday scenes (cafes, rivers, gardens), and light that feels like a specific time of day. If it looks blurry up close and glowing from across the room, that's it.

cards.q: What were the Impressionists mainly trying to capture?
cards.explain: They painted en plein air (outdoors), racing to catch fleeting light. Accuracy and narrative took a back seat to the sensation of the moment.

flashcards.back: Placing separate dabs of unblended color side by side so the viewer's eye mixes them.

flashcards.front: Why did Monet paint Rouen Cathedral 30+ times?
flashcards.back: To study how the same subject changes under different light, hours, and weather.

flashcards.front: Where did the name 'Impressionism' come from?
flashcards.back: A critic's insult — dismissing the works as 'just an impression' rather than finished paintings.

questions.q: What made Impressionist technique radical for its time?
choices: Painting quickly outdoors with visible, unblended strokes
questions.explain: The academy demanded invisible brushwork and studio polish. Painting fast, outside, with raw dabs of color broke every rule at once.

choices: The viewer's eye optically mixes adjacent dabs
The paint chemically blends on the canvas
questions.explain: It's optical mixing — blue and orange dabs side by side read as vibrating light. The blending happens in perception, not on the palette.

questions.q: Which subject would an Impressionist most likely paint?
choices: A sunlit riverside cafe at dusk
A formal royal portrait in a studio
questions.explain: Everyday modern life in fleeting light — cafes, rivers, gardens, stations. Formal portraiture was the establishment style they rejected.

choices: An independent show outside the official Salon
questions.explain: Rejected by the official Salon, they staged their own exhibition — the birth certificate of modern art's independent spirit.

questions.q: Post-Impressionists like Van Gogh and Seurat differed by:
choices: Pushing color and structure further, more deliberately
questions.explain: They kept the Impressionists' freedom with color but added structure and emotion — pointillist dots, swirling expression — pointing toward modern art.

cards.title: Art stops copying reality
cards.body: Modern art (roughly 1900-1970) asked a dangerous question: what if art doesn't have to look like anything? Photography could capture reality perfectly, so painters went the other way — into emotion, ideas, dreams, and pure shape. Cubism, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism: each broke reality a little more.

cards.title: Cubism: every angle at once
cards.body: Picasso and Braque's Cubism shattered objects into geometric fragments and showed multiple viewpoints simultaneously — a face in profile and front view at the same time. It looks strange because it is: it's a rebellion against the single fixed viewpoint that perspective had enforced for 500 years.

Stand before Picasso's Guernica: screaming figures, a bull, a fallen horse, all in black, white, and grey, fractured across a 25-foot canvas. It depicts the bombing of a Spanish town — not photographically, but as pure anguish made visible. You don't need to 'get' the shapes to feel it.

When modern art confuses you, ask three questions: what was the artist reacting against, what feeling does it give you before you think, and what would be lost if it looked 'normal'? Confusion is often the intended first step, not a failure.

cards.q: Why did modern artists move away from realistic depiction?
choices: Photography handled realism, freeing art to explore emotion and ideas
They forgot how to paint realistically
cards.explain: Once cameras captured reality effortlessly, realistic painting lost its monopoly. Artists pivoted to what cameras couldn't do: inner experience, concepts, pure form.

flashcards.back: Breaking objects into geometric fragments showing multiple viewpoints at once (Picasso, Braque).
The bombing of the Spanish town of Guernica — anguish made visible in fractured black, white, and grey.

flashcards.front: Three questions to ask when modern art confuses you?
flashcards.back: What was the artist reacting against? What do I feel first? What would be lost if it looked 'normal'?

questions.q: Cubism broke with 500 years of tradition by:
questions.explain: Since the Renaissance, paintings used one fixed viewpoint. Cubism smashed that — profile and frontal views coexist in a single fractured image.

questions.q: Surrealism (Dalí, Magritte) drew its imagery mainly from:
questions.explain: Surrealists mined dreams, free association, and Freud's unconscious — melting clocks and bowler-hatted men are dream logic on canvas.

questions.q: Abstract Expressionism (Pollock, Rothko) is best described as:
choices: Non-representational painting focused on gesture, color, and emotion
questions.explain: Drip paintings and floating color fields depict nothing recognizable — the painting is the record of an act, or a field of pure feeling.

questions.q: Pop Art (Warhol) differed from Abstract Expressionism by:
choices: Embracing mass culture and commercial imagery
questions.explain: Warhol's soup cans and Marilyns dragged advertising and celebrity into galleries — high art made from low culture, deliberately.

questions.q: A good first response to confusing modern art is:
choices: Notice what you feel before analyzing what it means
Assume it's a fraud and walk away
questions.explain: Modern art often targets feeling before intellect. Your raw reaction is data, not ignorance — start there, then investigate.
